name: Kanban Board with WIP Limits
use_case: Our team has far too much work open at once: each of us picks up the next request before the last one is done, so dozens of items sit half-finished and hardly anything gets completed. Every item goes on a card on a shared board with one column per stage, the team agrees a maximum number of cards allowed in each working column, a new item is pulled in only when another has moved on, and the team regularly looks at where cards pile up.
strengths: makes all open work and its stage visible to everyone at once, instead of being spread across personal lists and inboxes
the limit on cards per column forces the team to finish or unblock work before starting more, which shortens the time each item takes
a column that keeps filling up shows where the real bottleneck is, so the team can help there instead of starting new work elsewhere
starts from the process the team already has: no new roles, sprints or meetings are required to begin
works with a wall and sticky notes or any online board, and fits offices, service desks and project groups as well as software teams
weaknesses: a board without agreed limits is only a shared to-do list; the effect depends on the team actually refusing to start work when a column is full
choosing the limits is guesswork at first and has to be adjusted over several weeks; there is no reliable rule for the right number
the board only reflects reality if everyone moves their cards; a stale board misleads more than no board
it does not decide which request matters most or set deadlines; ordering the queue needs a separate agreement or method
teams that cannot say no to incoming requests, because a manager or another unit keeps pushing work in, hit the limits at once and need backing from above
the evidence for knowledge work is mostly practitioner reports and case studies; reviews note few rigorous studies and almost no published failures
use_cases: We take on new work faster than we finish it: half-done items pile up, and whatever waits for a colleague's input or a sign-off lies forgotten until somebody chases it.

A school's administration team handles enrolment forms, room bookings and parent letters in parallel; each person has twenty requests open, several wait days for a teacher's signature, and the team lead only finds out when someone chases them.

A municipal service desk handles permit questions and requests from other departments arriving by e-mail, phone and at the counter; each clerk has many half-processed files open at once, begins whatever arrived last, and files waiting for another office are forgotten.

A small communications team writes posts, flyers, newsletters and press texts and works on fifteen of them in parallel; each piece is late because it sits waiting for a draft, feedback or sign-off that no one is tracking.

A nonprofit project group made up partly of volunteers: people say they will take on a job and then it sits untouched for weeks, while the coordinator cannot see which jobs are actually moving and which have quietly stalled.
